scope: A bounded immune-mediated podocytopathy map of primary minimal change nephropathy: anti-nephrin autoantibodies with humoral and Th2 associations, T-cell and cytokine (IL-8, IL-13) observations, experimental antibody and IL-13 models, foot-process effacement and nephrotic syndrome. Excludes secondary causes, genetics, other glomerulopathies and treatment efficacy; CD80, CTLA-4 and ANGPTL4 evidence is not yet curated.

paragraphs.text: Primary minimal change disease (MCD) is represented here as an immune-associated podocytopathy with heterogeneous upstream pathogenesis, foot-process effacement and nephrotic proteinuria. Anti-nephrin autoantibodies identify a subset: one multicentre cohort detected them in 44% of adults with MCD and 69% with active untreated disease. Levels tracked activity and proteinuria, fell during remission and reappeared before relapse; prevalence varies by assay and cohort. Human biopsy findings associate antibodies with podocyte IgG. Nephrin immunization in mice induced an MCD-like syndrome, nephrin phosphorylation and podocyte cytoskeletal changes. Patient IgG transferred to a rabbit caused proteinuria, effacement without deposits and nephrin phosphorylation. These experiments support a pathogenic antibody route in selected systems, without establishing each intracellular step or explaining antibody-negative disease. Anti-nephrin-positive patients also had IgG4 predominance, Th2-skewed cytokines and a non-significant plasmablast trend; their sequence is unresolved. A newly added human study found higher hemopexin protease activity despite lower hemopexin concentration during MCD relapse, compared with remission. This supplies a separate observational circulating-factor signal, not proof that hemopexin causes human MCD.

The antibody-transfer experiment used total IgG from one patient in one rabbit, rather than purified nephrin-specific antibody; animal sufficiency does not establish universal human necessity. The hemopexin study compared 18 relapsing patients, 23 patients in remission after prednisolone, other glomerulopathies and controls; treatment and disease-stage confounding remain. Its kidney-tissue activity assay did not establish in vivo permeability-factor causation. Peripheral CD4 activation at onset remains an association. IL-13 overexpression in rats caused albuminuria, foot-process fusion and changes in nephrin and B7-1 expression, supporting a model-specific route without establishing that IL-13 is necessary in humans. Urinary IL-8 rose in relapse, yet that study did not support a disease-specific pathogenic role for IL-8 or TNF-alpha under its tested conditions. No single upstream factor is established as necessary or sufficient across primary MCD. Concurrent steroid-induced remission and antibody clearance do not isolate the mediator of treatment response. Secondary causes, other glomerulopathies and treatment efficacy are excluded from this synthesis. Human observations and animal experiments retain separate graph contexts; most sources, including the newly added hemopexin report, were inspected at abstract level. Independent domain review and calibrated appraisals remain pending.
